title: The missing property
summary: Repair a TypeScript data model and a function that reads it.

scenario.briefing: An order type claims orders have only an id and customer name. The API sends items, and itemCount crashes. Extend the model and make the function sum quantities.

objectives.description: Describe the items array in the Order interface.
Return the total quantity across items.

hints: An order item has a quantity, and the order holds an array of items.
Add items to the interface with a type of { quantity: number }[].
itemCount must add every quantity, not just count array entries.
interface OrderItem { quantity: number } interface Order { id: string; customerName: string; items: OrderItem[]; } Then loop and sum item.quantity.

misconceptions.description: Counting item rows instead of quantities.
misconceptions.feedback: An item row can have quantity 3. The total must sum quantities, not count rows.

misconceptions.description: Expecting a TypeScript interface to validate runtime JSON.
misconceptions.feedback: Interfaces are erased at runtime. They describe code to the compiler; external JSON still needs runtime validation.

sections.title: Objects group related facts
sections.body: An order contains an id, a customer name, and a list of items. Each item has a name and quantity. Objects make those relationships explicit, and arrays hold repeated values such as items.

sections.title: Types describe expectations
sections.body: TypeScript checks that code uses declared properties consistently. Interfaces disappear from the running program, so they cannot validate incoming JSON by themselves. A runtime schema is still needed at a trust boundary.

vocabulary.definition: A named description of an object's properties and types.
A named value inside an object.
Removal of type information when compiling to JavaScript.

steps.title: Repair the order model
steps.prompt: Edit order.ts. Extend Order with items, define an item type, and make itemCount return the summed quantity. Run the tests.

tests.description: An order with no items totals zero.
tests.name: itemCount

tests.description: Item quantity is typed as a number.

steps.title: Do types validate JSON?
steps.prompt: The API sends an order where items is a string. The TypeScript interface says items is an array. What happens at runtime after compilation?

options.label: The program runs without an automatic interface check; the bad data can still break the function.
TypeScript throws a validation error at runtime.
The interface converts the string into an array.
The network request is rejected before JavaScript runs.

quiz.explanation: Interfaces are erased. Runtime validation of external data must be implemented with a schema or explicit checks.

hints: Think about what remains after TypeScript compiles.
Interfaces are not present in the JavaScript output.
Nothing automatically checks the JSON shape.
The program runs and the bad data can cause a runtime failure.

steps.title: Types and trust boundaries

statements.label: Types catch some mistakes before the program runs.
Interfaces alone do not validate external JSON.
Runtime data still needs validation at trust boundaries.
A compiled TypeScript program cannot have runtime errors.

steps.explanation: Static types and runtime validation solve different problems. Both are needed at boundaries.
